name: Resting heart rate
what: How many times your heart beats per minute at rest.
why_in_space: Fluid shifts toward the head and the heart works differently without gravity. Stress and poor sleep also raise resting heart rate.
how_to_measure: Rest for 5 minutes, restrained and still.
Wear the chest strap or use the pulse oximeter.
Record the value after it settles for 30 seconds.
expected_change: A small change in resting heart rate in the first weeks of flight is a normal adaptation.

source.citation: PLACEHOLDER: general adult clinical range. Replace with NASA-STD-3001 / HRP evidence report.

name: Blood pressure (systolic)
what: The pressure in your arteries when the heart beats.
why_in_space: Fluid shift, altered gravity, sleep debt and stress all affect blood pressure.
how_to_measure: Rest for 5 minutes.
Anchor your arm at heart level; in microgravity it will float.
Fit the cuff on the bare upper arm and start the monitor.
Stay still and silent until it finishes.
expected_change: Blood pressure often runs slightly lower in microgravity than on Earth.

source.citation: PLACEHOLDER: general adult clinical range. Replace with NASA-STD-3001 / HRP evidence report.

actions.text: Protect tonight's sleep block: no late tasks, use the sleep mask.

name: Blood pressure (diastolic)
what: The pressure in your arteries between heartbeats.
why_in_space: Fluid shift, altered gravity, sleep debt and stress all affect blood pressure.
how_to_measure: Measured together with systolic pressure by the cuff.

source.citation: PLACEHOLDER: general adult clinical range. Replace with NASA-STD-3001 / HRP evidence report.

name: Body temperature
what: Your core temperature, a quick sign of infection or heat stress.
why_in_space: The immune system changes in flight and a closed cabin spreads germs easily.
how_to_measure: Use the thermometer as its card shows.
Wait 15 minutes after exercise, food or drink.
expected_change: Core temperature can run slightly higher during long missions.

source.citation: PLACEHOLDER: general adult clinical range. Replace with NASA-STD-3001 / HRP evidence report.

actions.text: Apply a cold pack and rest.

name: Blood glucose
what: The amount of sugar in your blood: your body's fuel level.
why_in_space: A limited food system and changed metabolism make nutrition a tracked risk on long missions.
how_to_measure: Wash and dry your hands.
Use the lancet and place the drop on the strip.
Note whether you ate in the last 2 hours.

source.citation: PLACEHOLDER: general adult clinical range. Replace with NASA-STD-3001 / HRP evidence report.

actions.text: If low: take glucose tabs as the kit card says, recheck in 15 minutes.
Eat your scheduled meal; do not skip it.

name: Blood oxygen (SpO2)
what: How much oxygen your blood is carrying.
why_in_space: Cabin air is recycled; CO2 build-up or a life-support fault shows up in the crew first.
how_to_measure: Warm your finger.
Clip the pulse oximeter on and hold still for 30 seconds.

source.citation: PLACEHOLDER: general adult clinical range. Replace with NASA-STD-3001 / HRP evidence report.

actions.text: Move to a well-ventilated module, check the cabin CO2 reading, recheck.

name: Sleep
what: Hours slept in the last sleep period.
why_in_space: No day-night cycle, noise, workload and shifted schedules cut sleep. Sleep debt affects mood, heart and performance.
how_to_measure: Log when you fell asleep and woke, or sync your wearable.
expected_change: Crews commonly sleep less in flight than on Earth.

source.citation: PLACEHOLDER: general sleep guidance. Replace with HRP sleep-loss evidence report.

actions.text: Use the sleep mask and dim the cabin 1 hour before sleep.

name: Mood
what: How you feel today, from 1 (very low) to 5 (very good).
why_in_space: Isolation, confinement and distance from home are a named NASA hazard for behavioural health.
how_to_measure: Answer the daily check-in honestly. Only you and the flight surgeon see it.
expected_change: Mood often dips around the middle of a long mission.

source.citation: PLACEHOLDER: self-report scale, not a clinical instrument.

actions.text: Talk to a crewmate you trust.
Request a private conference with ground.

name: Stress
what: How calm you feel today, from 1 (very stressed) to 5 (calm).
why_in_space: High workload and confinement raise stress, which also affects sleep and the heart.
how_to_measure: Answer the daily check-in.

source.citation: PLACEHOLDER: self-report scale, not a clinical instrument.

actions.text: Take a 10-minute break and do the breathing exercise.

name: Radiation dose rate
what: How much radiation your personal dosimeter recorded in the last day.
why_in_space: Outside Earth's magnetic field, cosmic rays and solar storms raise long-term cancer and tissue risk.
how_to_measure: Read the daily value from your personal dosimeter.
During a solar storm alert, move to the shelter first.
expected_change: A steady background dose is expected in deep space.
